lines: One record nobody can process, retried right where it sits, and the whole line behind it just stops.
Nothing downstream is broken. It's simply waiting on something that will never actually succeed.
That backlog doesn't shrink on its own, either. It only grows.
An earlier fix assumed a repeat could eventually be caught, given enough patience.
It never assumed a record could fail forever, no matter how many times anyone tries it.
And since this kind of ordering only promises anything within one lane, stalling that lane stalls everyone sharing it.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Instead of trying the stuck record again right where it jammed, move it somewhere else entirely.
Does everyone waiting behind it get to keep moving, or are they still stuck too?
answer: They keep moving, almost right away.
Once that one record is somebody else's problem, nothing in the original lane is waiting on it anymore.
So everything behind it simply resumes, as if it had never jammed at all.

lines: Move the stuck record off to its own separate lane, and the original one has nothing left to wait for.
Everyone behind it starts moving again, immediately.
The jam is gone, just not solved yet.
That fix isn't free, and it's worth naming plainly what it actually costs.
The detour is a slower road, so whatever travels it tends to arrive later than things that never left the main lane.
Order, in other words, is the price of not getting stuck.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Picture a record moving through several lanes, each one giving it a little longer to wait before trying again.
It fails every single one of them, with nothing left after the last. What happens to it then?
answer: It lands somewhere specific, not nowhere.
A dedicated resting place for exactly this situation, carrying enough about the record to actually make sense of it later.
Not an infinite loop, and not quietly thrown away either.

lines: That resting place only earns its keep if someone can actually use what it's carrying.
Where it came from, what went wrong trying it, and how many times that was already tried.
Without all three, nobody fixing the problem later has enough to go on.
This isn't some improvised workaround someone bolted on after the fact.
One widely used connector framework has it built right into its own error-handling setting.
And a newer release of a popular stream-processing library added the exact same idea as a first-class feature.
Every figure in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy models.
The jam that really stopped cold, and the detour that really kept the rest of the line moving.
And a real record, carrying everything someone would actually need to track the failure back down.
So: never retry a record that can't succeed right where it jammed everyone else.
Move it aside instead, and say out loud what that costs in ordering.
And give whatever ends up stuck enough about itself that somebody can actually bring it back.
